title: The lump of salt dissolved — no inside, no outside (2.4)
hook: Yajnavalkya drops salt in water, says there's no awareness after death, and Maitreyi says: now you've confused me
tomorrow: the honey doctrine — all beings are honey for each other

segments.voice: Yesterday, nididhyasana: the self is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated on. Hear, reflect, dwell. Your line was for the sake of the self.

A lump of salt, dropped into water overnight. In the morning it's gone, yet every sip is salty, here, and here. Twenty days ago, in the Chandogya, a father used that salt to teach his son. Today, in a different book, a different teacher picks it up: Yajnavalkya, still talking with Maitreyi. And this time the salt says something she can't follow. She tells him so, out loud. Here, sir, you've confused me.
screen: `SALT IN WATER, AGAIN.` → `A DIFFERENT TEACHER.` → `HERE, SIR, YOU'VE CONFUSED ME.`

segments.voice: As a lump of salt thrown into water dissolves, he says, and you can't pick it out again, but wherever you take the water from it's salty, so this great being, endless, without limit, is nothing but a mass of knowing. It rises up out of these elements, and vanishes back into them. Then the hard line: after death, there is no awareness. Maitreyi stops him. That's where you've confused me. She's not slow. It sounds as if the deathless self she asked for just dissolved into nothing. Yajnavalkya says: I'm saying nothing confusing. Listen. Where there seems to be two, one sees another, hears another, knows another. But where everything has become one's own self, then by what, and whom, would one see? By what would one know the knower? So the salt isn't gone. It's everywhere. What ends is the gap between a knower and something known. When the scene is told again later in the book, the salt image grows sharper, and gives today its title: a lump of salt has no inside and no outside; it's taste all the way through. So this self has no inside, no outside; it's knowing all the way through. Schools of Vedanta read the dissolving differently. For Advaita, the separate knower melts like the salt, and only pure consciousness is left. Other schools read that line, no awareness after death, as the end of the narrow, body-bound kind of knowing, not of the soul itself. Neither reading turns the self into nothing. Maitreyi's confusion is the right question, asked out loud.
screen: `SALT DISSOLVES; THE WATER IS SALTY.` · `AFTER DEATH, NO AWARENESS.` · `BY WHAT WOULD ONE KNOW THE KNOWER?` · `NO INSIDE, NO OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `PURE CONSCIOUSNESS.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you: a car, a fan, your own breath. Notice that you can't find the edge where a sound stops being out there and starts being heard in here; it's hearing, all the way through. When a thought builds the wall again, me in here, the world out there, let it dissolve like the salt.
Vijnanaghana, a mass of knowing. Gone from sight, yet taste all the way through: the self, knowing all the way through, like a dissolved lump of salt.
Your line: pure consciousness. Tomorrow, the honey teaching, and a sage with a horse's head. That's day three hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Teachers of Vedanta use the salt image, from both the Chandogya and the Brihadaranyaka, to explain how the self pervades everything; this passage is read and debated in Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita commentaries alike.

fork.setup: you're Maitreyi. your husband says that after death there is no awareness. what do you do?
options: tell him plainly: here, you've confused me.
decide he doesn't know after all.
fork.reveal: she says it out loud, and he explains: where all has become the self, by what would one see whom? by what would one know the knower?

original.note: Sanskrit vijñāna (knowing) + ghana (solid, dense): a mass of knowing, like a lump of salt.

trapdoor: what you thought: after death there's nothing.
what it means: where everything has become the self, there's no second thing to see or know, only knowing all the way through.
what a scholar hears: the scene appears twice; 2.4.12 has salt dissolving in water, 4.5.13 the lump with no inside or outside. schools differ on what the no awareness ends.

chat.says: If the self dissolves like salt, doesn't that mean it's just gone after death?
options: No, the salt isn't gone, it's everywhere; what ends is the gap between knower and known.
Yes, Yajnavalkya teaches that nothing at all is left of a person after death.
Yes, and that's why Maitreyi gave up on the teaching and took her share.
chat.meaning: Yajnavalkya says the salt isn't gone but everywhere: where all has become one's own self, the gap between a knower and something known ends.

vijnanaghana.meaning: a mass of knowing, knowing all the way through

Chandogya.meaning: the Upanishad where Uddalaka taught his son with salt

Maitreyi.meaning: Yajnavalkya's wife, who asked for the deathless

Vedanta.meaning: the schools that teach from the Upanishads

Advaita.meaning: the not-two school of Vedanta: one self in all

'No inside, no outside… a mass of taste / knowing' is from 4.5.13 (the second telling), where the word is prajñānaghana; the script uses vijñānaghana from 2.4.12. Confirm.
